blocks.p: In my travels, as I walked through many regions and countries, I happened by chance into that famous continent of Universe. A very large and spacious country it is. It lies between the two poles, right in the midst of the four points of the heavens. It is a well-watered place, richly adorned with hills and valleys, finely situated, and for the most part, at least where I was, very fruitful; it is also well peopled, and the air is very sweet.

The people are not all of one complexion, nor of one language, custom, or religion, but differ as much, it is said, as the planets themselves. Some are right and some are wrong, just as it happens in smaller regions.

In this country, as I said, it was my lot to travel; and travel there I did, for so long that I learned much of their mother tongue, along with the customs and manners of the people I was among. And to tell the truth, I was greatly delighted with many things I saw and heard among them. Indeed, I would surely have lived and died a native among them (so taken was I with them and their doings), had my master not sent for me to come home to his house, there to do business for him and to oversee business done.

Now there is in this fine country of Universe a fair and delicate town, a corporation called Mansoul, which is to say, a man’s soul: a town so curious in its building, so convenient in its situation, so advantageous in its privileges (I mean with reference to its origin), that I may say of it what was said before of the continent it stands in: there is not its equal under the whole heaven.

As for the situation of this town, it lies right between the two worlds. Its first founder and builder, so far as I can gather from the best and most authentic records, was one Shaddai, the King, whose name means the Almighty; and he built it for his own delight. He made it the mirror and glory of all that he made, the crowning piece, beyond anything else he did in that country. Indeed, so beautiful a town was Mansoul when it was first built that some say the mighty ones of heaven came down to see it set up, and sang for joy. And as he made it beautiful to look at, so he also made it mighty, to have dominion over all the country round about. All were commanded to acknowledge Mansoul as their capital; all were required to do it homage. Yes, the town itself had a clear commission and power from her King to demand service of everyone, and to subdue any who in any way refused it.

In the middle of this town there was raised a most famous and stately palace. For strength it might be called a castle; for pleasantness, a paradise; for size, a place so spacious it could hold the whole world. This place King Shaddai intended for himself alone, and for no one else with him: partly for his own delight, and partly because he did not want the terror of strangers to come upon the town. Shaddai also made this place a garrison, but he committed the keeping of it to the men of the town alone.

The walls of the town were so well built, so firmly knit together, that but for the townsmen themselves they could never have been shaken or broken. For here lay the excellent wisdom of the one who built Mansoul: the walls could never be broken down or harmed by the mightiest enemy power unless the townsmen consented to it.

This famous town of Mansoul had five gates to come in by and go out by, and these were made to match the walls: impregnable, and such as could never be opened or forced except by the will and permission of those inside. The names of the gates were these: Ear-gate, Eye-gate, Mouth-gate, Nose-gate, and Feel-gate.

Add to these some other things that belonged to Mansoul, and the glory and strength of the place will show still more. It always had enough provisions within its walls. It had the best, most wholesome, and most excellent law then in existence in the world. There was not a rascal, rogue, or traitor within its walls then; they were all true men, and firmly joined together, and that, as you know, is a great matter. And on top of all this, it always had (so long as it had the goodness to stay true to Shaddai the King) his favor and his protection, and it was his delight.

Well, once upon a time a certain Diabolus, a mighty giant, who is the Devil himself, made an assault on this famous town of Mansoul, to take it and make it his own dwelling. This giant was king of the powers of darkness, and a most raging prince he was. If you please, we will first speak of the origin of this Diabolus, and then of his taking of the town.

This Diabolus is indeed a great and mighty prince, and yet both poor and beggarly. As for his origin, he was at first one of the servants of King Shaddai, made by him, taken up, and set in a most high and mighty place; he was given principalities that belonged to the best of the King’s territories and dominions. This Diabolus was made “son of the morning” [Isa. 14:12], and a fine position he had of it. It brought him much glory and gave him much brightness, an income that might have contented his proud, Lucifer-like heart, if it had not been insatiable, and as wide as hell itself.

Well, seeing himself raised so high in greatness and honor, and raging in his mind for higher rank and station, what does he do but begin to plot how he might be set up as lord over all, and have the sole power under Shaddai. (Now that power the King had reserved for his Son; indeed, he had already given it to him.) So first he consulted with himself about what was best to be done, and then he opened his mind to some of his companions, and they agreed to it. In short, they came to this conclusion: that they should make an attempt on the King’s Son to destroy him, so that the inheritance might be theirs. Well, to be brief, the treason, as I said, was agreed on, the time set, the word given, the rebels gathered, and the assault attempted. Now the King and his Son, being all eye and always watching, could not fail to see everything that passed in his dominions; and since he always loved his Son as himself, he could not help being greatly provoked and offended at what he saw. So what does he do but catch them at the very first step they took toward their design. He convicts them of their treason, horrid rebellion, and conspiracy, and casts them out of every place of trust, benefit, honor, and promotion. That done, he banishes them from the court and turns them down into the horrible pits, bound fast in chains, never again to expect the least favor from his hands, but to await the judgment he had appointed, and that forever.

Now, cast out like this from every place of trust, profit, and honor, and knowing that they had lost their prince’s favor forever, you may be sure that they would now add to their former pride all the malice and rage against Shaddai and his Son that they could. So they roved and ranged in great fury from place to place, to see if they might find something that belonged to the King, so that by spoiling it they might take revenge on him. At last they happened into this spacious country of Universe and steered their course toward the town of Mansoul. And considering that this town was one of the chief works and delights of King Shaddai, what do they do but, after taking counsel, make an assault on it. I say they knew that Mansoul belonged to Shaddai, for they were there when he built it and beautified it for himself. So when they had found the place, they shouted horribly for joy and roared over it like a lion over its prey, saying, “Now we have found the prize, and the way to be revenged on King Shaddai for what he has done to us.” So they sat down and called a council of war, and considered how best to win this famous town of Mansoul for themselves. And these four questions were put forward to be considered:
First, whether they should all show themselves to the town of Mansoul in this undertaking.
Second, whether they should go and sit down before Mansoul in their present ragged and beggarly shape.
Third, whether they should show Mansoul their intentions and the design they had come about, or assault it with words and ways of deceit.

Fourth, whether they should give private orders to some of their companions to take any advantage they saw, and shoot one or more of the principal townsmen, if they judged that their cause and design would be better served by it.

1. To the first of these proposals the answer was no: it would not be best for all of them to show themselves before the town, because the appearance of many of them might alarm and frighten the town, whereas a few, or only one, would not be so likely to. And to press this advice home it was added that if Mansoul were frightened, or took alarm, “it is impossible,” said Diabolus (for he spoke now), “that we should take the town, since no one can enter it without its own consent. So let only a few, or only one, assault Mansoul; and in my opinion,” said Diabolus, “let me be the one.” And to this they all agreed.

2. Then they came to the second proposal, about their ragged and beggarly shape. To this too the answer was no, by no means; because, although the town of Mansoul had before now been made to know, and to have dealings with, things that are invisible, they had never yet seen any of their fellow creatures in so sad and wretched a condition as these. This was the advice of that fierce Alecto.

Then said Apollyon, “The advice is to the point. For even one of us appearing to them as we are now would be sure to breed and multiply such thoughts in them as would throw them into dismay and force them to put themselves on guard. And if so,” he said, “then, as my lord Diabolus said just now, it is useless for us to think of taking the town.”

Then said that mighty giant Beelzebub, “The advice already given is safe. For though the men of Mansoul have seen such beings as we once were, they have never yet seen such beings as we are now. And in my opinion it is best to come upon them in a shape that is common and familiar among them.”

When they had agreed to this, the next thing to consider was in what shape, color, or form Diabolus had best show himself when he set out to make Mansoul his own. Then one said one thing, and another the opposite. At last Lucifer answered that in his opinion it would be best for his lordship to take on the body of one of the creatures that the townspeople had dominion over. “For,” he said, “these are not only familiar to them, but being under them, they will never imagine that an attempt on the town could be made by one of them. And to blind them completely, let him take on the body of the beast that Mansoul thinks wiser than all the rest.” This advice was applauded by all; so it was decided that the giant Diabolus should take on the dragon, for in those days that creature was as familiar to the town of Mansoul as a bird is now to a boy; nothing in its first, unfallen state alarmed them in the least. Then they went on to the third question, which was:

3. Whether they should show their intentions, the design of his coming, to Mansoul or not. This too was answered no, because of the weight of the earlier reasons: namely, that Mansoul were a strong people, a strong people in a strong town, whose wall and gates were impregnable (to say nothing of their castle), and who could by no means be won except by their own consent.

“Besides,” said Legion (for he gave the answer to this one), “if they find out our intentions, they may send to their King for help; and if that happens, I know well enough what time of day it will be for us. So let us assault them with every show of fairness, covering our intentions with all kinds of lies, flatteries, and deluding words; pretending things that never will be, and promising them what they will never find. This is the way to win Mansoul, and to make them open their gates to us of their own accord; yes, and even beg us to come in. And the reason I think this plan will work is that the people of Mansoul are, every one of them, simple and innocent, all honest and true; they do not yet know what it is to be attacked with fraud, guile, and hypocrisy. They are strangers to lying and deceiving lips. So if we are disguised like this, they will not see through us at all. Our lies will pass for true sayings, and our pretenses for honest dealing. They will believe whatever we promise them, especially if, in all our lies and false words, we pretend great love for them, and make out that our design is only their advantage and honor.”
Now there was not one word of reply against this. It went down as smoothly as water runs down a steep slope. So they went on to consider the last proposal, which was:

4. Whether they should order some of their company to shoot one or more of the principal townsmen. This was carried in the affirmative, and the man marked out for destruction by this scheme was one Mr. Resistance, also called Captain Resistance. A great man in Mansoul this Captain Resistance was, and a man whom the giant Diabolus and his band feared more than all the rest of Mansoul put together. Now who should be the one to do the murder? That was the next question; and they appointed Tisiphone, a fury of the lake below, to do it.

Having ended their council of war, they rose up and set about doing what they had decided. They marched toward Mansoul, but all of them invisible except one, only one; and he did not approach the town in his own likeness, but under the cover and in the body of the dragon.

So they drew up and sat down before Ear-gate, for that was the place of hearing for everyone outside the town, as Eye-gate was the place of seeing. So, as I said, he came up with his followers to the gate, and laid his ambush for Captain Resistance within bowshot of the town. This done, the giant went up close to the gate, taking no one with him but one Mr. Dwell-on-it, his spokesman in all difficult matters, and, as the custom was in those days, sounded his trumpet to call the town of Mansoul to a hearing. At this the chief men of the town of Mansoul, such as my Lord Innocent, my Lord Willbewill (the town’s will), my Lord Mayor, Mr. Conscience, the Recorder (the town’s judge and the keeper of its law), and Captain Resistance, came down to the wall to see who was there and what the matter was. And when my Lord Willbewill had looked over and seen who stood at the gate, he demanded to know who he was, why he had come, and why he had roused the town of Mansoul with so unusual a sound.

Then Diabolus, as meek as a lamb, began his speech. “Gentlemen of the famous town of Mansoul,” he said, “I am, as you can see, no distant stranger, but a near neighbor, and one bound by the King to do you homage and whatever service I can. So, to be faithful both to myself and to you, I have something of importance to tell you. Grant me a hearing, then, and listen to me patiently. And first, I assure you that it is not myself but you, not my advantage but yours, that I am seeking by what I do now, as will be made perfectly plain once I have opened my mind to you. For, gentlemen, I have come (to tell you the truth) to show you how you may obtain a great and full deliverance from a bondage in which, without knowing it, you are held captive and enslaved.”
At this the town of Mansoul began to prick up its ears. “What is it? Please, what is it?” they thought.

And he said, “I have something to say to you about your King, about his law, and also about yourselves. As for your King, I know he is great and powerful; but all the same, what he has told you is neither true nor for your good.

“First, it is not true. For the thing he has held over you to keep you in awe will not come to pass, nor be fulfilled, even if you do what he has forbidden. But even if there were danger, what slavery it is to live always in fear of the greatest of punishments for doing so small and trivial a thing as eating a little fruit!

“Second, as for his laws, I say further that they are unreasonable, confusing, and intolerable. Unreasonable, as I hinted before, because the punishment is out of proportion to the offense: there is a great difference between a life and an apple, and yet by the law of your Shaddai the one must go for the other. They are confusing too, because first he says you may eat of everything, and afterward forbids you to eat of one. And last of all, they must be intolerable, since the fruit you are forbidden to eat (if you are forbidden any) is the one thing, and the only thing, that by your eating it could bring you a good you do not yet know. This is plain from the very name of the tree: it is called ‘the tree of the knowledge of good and evil’ [Gen. 2:17]. And do you have that knowledge yet? No, no; nor can you imagine how good, how pleasant, and how much to be desired to make one wise it is, so long as you stand by your King’s commandment. Why should you be held in ignorance and blindness? Why should you not be enlarged in knowledge and understanding?

“And now, you inhabitants of the famous town of Mansoul, to speak more particularly about yourselves: you are not a free people! You are kept in bondage and slavery, and that by a heavy threat, with no reason given but ‘So I will have it; so it shall be.’ And is it not painful to think that the very thing you are forbidden to do, if only you would do it, would yield you both wisdom and honor? For then your eyes will be opened, and you will be like gods [Gen. 3:5]. Now, since this is so,” he said, “could any prince keep you in more slavery and greater bondage than you are in this day? You are made underlings, and wrapped up in hardships, as I have clearly shown. For what bondage is greater than to be kept blind? Won’t reason tell you that it is better to have eyes than to be without them, and so better to be at liberty than to be shut up in a dark and stinking cave?”

And just then, while Diabolus was speaking these words to Mansoul, Tisiphone shot at Captain Resistance where he stood on the gate and wounded him mortally in the head; so that, to the amazement of the townsmen and the encouragement of Diabolus, he fell down dead right over the wall. Now when Captain Resistance was dead (and he was the only soldier in the town), poor Mansoul was left wholly stripped of courage, with no heart left to resist. But this was just as the devil would have it. Then Mr. Dwell-on-it, the spokesman Diabolus had brought with him, stood up and addressed the town. His speech went like this.

“Gentlemen,” he said, “it is my master’s happiness that he has a quiet and teachable audience today, and we hope we shall persuade you not to throw away good advice. My master has a very great love for you; and although he knows very well that he runs the risk of King Shaddai’s anger, his love for you will make him do more than that. Nor is there any need for another word to confirm the truth of what he has said. There is not a word of it that does not carry its own proof within it; the very name of the tree may put an end to all argument on the matter. So at this time, with my lord’s permission,” and with that he made Diabolus a very low bow, “I will add only this advice: consider his words; look at the tree and its promising fruit; remember too that you still know only a little, and that this is the way to know more. And if your reason is not won over to accept such good counsel, you are not the men I took you for.”

But when the townsfolk saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was pleasant to the eyes, and a tree to be desired to make one wise, they did as old Dwell-on-it advised: they took of its fruit and ate [Gen. 3:6]. I should have told you before that even while Dwell-on-it was speaking, my Lord Innocent sank down where he stood and could not be brought back to life; whether from a shot from the giant’s camp, or from some sickly faintness that suddenly came over him, or from the stinking breath of that treacherous villain old Dwell-on-it, which is what I am most inclined to think. So these two brave men died. Brave men, I call them, for they were the beauty and glory of Mansoul as long as they lived there. And now there was no noble spirit left in Mansoul. They all fell down and yielded obedience to Diabolus, and became his slaves and servants, as you will hear.

Now, with these two dead, what do the rest of the townsfolk do but, like men who had found a fool’s paradise, set about at once, as I hinted before, to prove the truth of the giant’s words. First they did as Dwell-on-it had taught them: they looked, they considered, they were taken with the forbidden fruit; they took some and ate; and having eaten, they immediately became drunk with it. So they opened the gates, both Ear-gate and Eye-gate, and let in Diabolus with all his bands, quite forgetting their good Shaddai, his law, and the judgment he had attached, with a solemn warning, to the breaking of it.

Diabolus, once inside the gates, marched up to the middle of the town to make his conquest as sure as he could. And finding by this time that the people’s affections were warmly inclining toward him, he thought it best to strike while the iron was hot, and made them this further deceitful speech:

“Alas, my poor Mansoul! I have done you this service, it is true: I have raised you to honor and enlarged your liberty. But alas, alas, poor Mansoul, now you need someone to defend you! For you may be sure that when Shaddai hears what has been done, he will come; for he will be sorry that you have broken his bonds and thrown off his cords. What will you do? Now that you have been set free, will you let your privileges be invaded and taken away? Or what will you resolve?”

Then they all with one consent said to this bramble, “Come and reign over us.” [Judg. 9:14] So he accepted the offer and became the king of the town of Mansoul. That done, the next thing was to give him possession of the castle, and with it the whole strength of the town. So into the castle he went: the castle Shaddai had built in Mansoul for his own delight and pleasure, now become a den and stronghold for the giant Diabolus.

Now, having taken possession of this stately palace or castle, what does he do but make it a garrison for himself, and strengthen and fortify it with all kinds of provisions against King Shaddai, and against anyone who might try to win it back for him and bring it under his obedience again.
